description: We are a team of passionate engineering students with skills in AI/ML, software development, data science, and problem-solving. We aim to transform NASA’s open data into innovative, practical solutions for real-world challenges. We believe in teamwork, creativity, rapid prototyping, and learning while building impactful technology that can make a difference on Earth and beyond.

details:
FieldShift Rotation Advisor is a decision-support web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations that protect soil, conserve water and cope with a changing climate.

What it does and how it works. A farmer picks any location on an interactive 3D Earth (or types coordinates), sets four priorities on a 1 to 5 scale (water conservation, soil health, income stability, heat and drought resilience) and enters the crops grown in the last two seasons. The app retrieves about 15 years of daily NASA POWER climate data for that point (temperature, rainfall, sunlight) and calculates indicators such as yearly rainfall against the 15-year normal, hot days above 35°C, rainfall variability and dry spells. It also loads local soil properties (clay, sand, organic carbon, pH) from ISRIC SoilGrids, and the farmer can enter their own lab values instead. [Edit to match what your app does when SoilGrids is unavailable.] A crop table of traits (water need, heat and drought tolerance, nitrogen fixation, plant family) feeds a rotation engine. The engine generates three-season rotations, removes agronomically invalid ones (for example the same plant family back to back, or no legume or cover crop), and scores the rest with a transparent weighted formula. The top three rotations are compared with the farmer’s current practice, each with a plain-language explanation. Further pages offer a climate what-if simulator, a 3D farm view, an AI agronomist assistant and downloadable reports. [Delete any module that is not working.]

Benefits and intended impact. Farmers must plan rotations seasons ahead while rainfall and heat become less predictable and soils decline. FieldShift turns open NASA data and local soil information into ranked, explainable options that favor water-saving crops, legumes and cover crops, and shows how plans hold up in warmer or drier conditions. It is free to run, needs only a location, and works anywhere on Earth.

Tools used. Python and Streamlit for the app; pandas and NumPy for analysis; Plotly for charts; Folium for maps [and NASA GIBS imagery, if used]; Globe.gl and Three.js for the 3D Earth and farm scene [only if used]; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface; the Google Gemini API for the assistant [only if used]. No special hardware is needed; it runs in a web browser. We used AI coding assistants (Google Antigravity and Gemini) to help write code and design the interface under our direction.

Creativity. Farmers aim at their field on a cockpit-style 3D globe. Their own priorities steer the ranking, every recommendation explains why, and what-if tests show how it changes under climate stress.

Factors considered. The tool is decision support, not a yield forecast. NASA POWER is satellite- and model-derived data at coarse resolution, so it describes a location’s climate and not a single field. The crop table holds approximate values that should be confirmed locally, and soil values should be checked with a lab test. Data sources and assumptions are labeled in the app. Next steps: NASA SMAP soil moisture, NDVI vegetation data, climate projections, and validation with agronomists and farmers.
